scope: Authored text, not a fresh source check of the final stack. All fronts retained to check whether a PR-131 consequence appears elsewhere. Only PR-131 descendants are audited.

episodes.takeaway: CLI chooses syntax, workspace and environment. Daemon owns execution machinery; an injected host module still supplies the command program. Renderer formats lifecycle reports.

Core takes source caching, revision/index publication and project membership. TypeScript keeps parsing, projects, source handles and reversible toolchain mutations. These are separate publication boundaries.

One retained core session can serve another request. Six query stores empty together after successful refresh or at release. TypeScript owns their keys and algorithms; backend release now awaits project cleanup.
after: Service owns one core scope + six handles

episodes.takeaway: A frozen, complete daemon policy crosses process and worker boundaries. Required slices replace scattered defaults. Closed failure/rejection vocabularies own precedence and retry meaning; the first failed admission guard wins.
Framing, validation, bounded exchanges, outbound mechanics and inbound serving become separate owners. Decoder lifetime is one connection; raw socket closure alone cannot decide request retry safety.
Result-fetch keeps one capture and durable record offset. Execute reattachment keeps request identity but starts a new capture and fetch budget. Accepted failure is not a signal to rerun locally.
before: CLI output store reused for warm output

episodes.takeaway: The ledger owns immutable acceptance identity. An execution session coordinates the FIFO queue, worker, delivery and resource sampling. A generation manager fences replaced workers; activity is projected from snapshots.

A delivery session coordinates attachments, retained output, acknowledgement and traces. Ledger state and spool bytes keep their owners. Stream completion, logical ACK and physical cleanup are distinct boundaries.

#148 stages package mechanisms while CLI still runs a frozen compatibility graph. #149 switches CLI to DaemonClient and removes app copies. Tests move to package internals or a read-only inspector; some observations narrow.
before: #148: package added; CLI graph still active

fronts.statement: The protocol moves from generation 4 to 5. commandName participates in duplicate compatibility; a mixed-generation peer takes compatibility handling before execution.
fronts.reason: PR #132 ties the version change to authoritative command metadata.

fronts.statement: The host executor returns ordered stdout/stderr bytes and an exit code. The worker validates module/results, rechunks, sequences and acknowledges durable consumption; diagnostics remain JSON-like and resource sampling has no host payload.
fronts.reason: PR #135 assigns protocol mechanics to the worker while keeping the daemon independent of CLI/core.

fronts.statement: CLI opens a workspace before command validation, prepares after validation, and falls back to local command handling when workspace resolution fails. State paths resolve once, including symlinked existing ancestors and missing tails.
fronts.reason: PRs #128–129 preserve observable error/read order and the same canonical state string; the architecture plan preserves local routing errors.

fronts.statement: Lifecycle text/JSON bytes move to renderer; CLI still selects format, writes bytes and wraps existing errors. Telemetry remains a leaf receiving the resolved path.
fronts.reason: PRs #129 and #136 specify these ownership boundaries and output preservation.

fronts.statement: One frozen command tuple supplies runtime validation and the union; an exhaustive CLI record separates workspace commands from help/version/control/unknown routes. Environment/home values are injected for isolated path tests; lifecycle formatting uses one stateless class.
fronts.reason: PRs #129, #132 and #136 explain deterministic tests, syntax ownership and the cohesive rendering unit.

fronts.statement: The state-directory layer also changes tests: a worker fixture waits for three files; startup-owner assertions tolerate transient missing reads and poll full owner identity, with 5-s ownership and 15-s readiness waits. That status scenario is later removed from the CLI suite.
fronts.reason: The #129 commits name synchronization/oracle stabilization. No separate reason was found for including these test changes in path ownership or for the exact waits. #149’s retirement is shown in episode 09.

fronts.statement: A FileSystem facade caches source bytes by absolute path + change token and replaces snapshot coverage, even for selection. Unchanged tracked files reuse bytes; changed/omitted files lose bytes; untracked reads pass through without retention.
fronts.reason: PR #123 preserves replacement and selection eviction, defers selection-aware retention, and keeps filesystem injection usable by existing services.

fronts.statement: Prepared state treats workspace refresh as replacement and selection as an overlay. Validation precedes toolchain commit, then one index assignment; failures invoke rollback. ensureFiles keeps earlier one-file progress if a later file fails.
fronts.reason: PR #124 explains incremental preparation, pre-commit validation and sequential progress.

fronts.statement: Core validates canonical membership and every active input; a fresh rebuild observes missing inputs and drops unreachable observations. FIFO config discovery keeps all project owners in order; the LAST configured owner is primary, with inferred fallback.
fronts.reason: Validation/collector reasons are stated in #126. No separate reason for last-owner precedence was found; commits explicitly characterize and publish the order.

fronts.statement: A failed portable candidate leaves its prior index/graph published. This is not a transaction across source bytes, graph and all backends: TypeScript refresh touches the source snapshot before graph and index preparation.
fronts.reason: The per-owner transaction is stated. The plan does not separately reconcile whole-refresh failure with these already-progressed owners.

fronts.statement: TypeScript journals source updates/removals and stages paths reversibly to preserve exact SourceFile and node handles. Core retains unchanged prepared/declaration identities rather than rebuilding every object.
fronts.reason: PR #124 explicitly preserves source/node identity and keeps ts-morph mutation ownership in TypeScript.

fronts.statement: The service owns one scope instance and six separate stores: definitions, references, targets, callers, callees and positions. Five store promises; positions store locations. Keys and query algorithms stay in TypeScript.
fronts.reason: PR #127 preserves independent key/value spaces, identities and algorithms.

fronts.statement: Cache undefined by presence; store the exact returned value/promise. A synchronous factory throw is not inserted; a rejected promise stays cached. Reset empties stores without cancelling issued promises or destroying handles. Reference projections and position-node lookups still happen outside stored results.
fronts.reason: Map.has and preserving existing identities/failure behavior are stated. No separate rationale was located for the minimal exported handle API or each preserved projection choice.

fronts.statement: Only successful refresh begins a new semantic turn, even if revisions are unchanged. Failed refresh retains semantic answers; it does not roll back every earlier owner. Release clears synchronously, then awaits projects; rejection propagates through backend release.
fronts.reason: PR #127 explains clear-first and success-only invalidation and discloses an awaited backend barrier.

fronts.statement: The async release barrier changes completion relative to main when project release is asynchronous. The PR discloses the await; why that contract is compatible with the architecture plan’s unchanged timing/failure promise is UNEXPLAINED.
fronts.reason: Inspected: supplied PR body/commit messages, exact main/tip sources and architecture/follow-up specs. Concrete TypeScript project cleanup is synchronous; the pending probe injects an async project.

fronts.statement: Session retention reuses discovery; cold request retention does not. Selection discovers freshly to avoid siblings. Backends are copied/frozen; each turn gets a fresh router. Open precedes validation, preparation follows it. Concurrent Promise.all release leaves the session reusable; later calls retry every backend.
fronts.reason: PR #128 explains discovery isolation, router lifetime, observable error/read ordering and repeatable release.

fronts.statement: The #127 delta adds six service and four scope cases without editing the five old service test bodies. Delayed release tests pin pending/rejection behavior; delayed-success and daemon scheduling are not new witnesses in that six-file diff.
fronts.reason: Tests characterize the chosen boundary; no separate explanation for those particular omissions was found. This page records a controlled delayed-success main/tip probe.

fronts.statement: Seven policy families cover transport, startup, shutdown, delivery, output, resources and diagnostics. Values are derived once, frozen and exactly validated across hops; no user flags/environment/config tune them. Serialization/override factories end package-internal; AST, declaration, runtime, manifest and dependency checks enforce that surface.
fronts.reason: Architecture and policy plans require one complete snapshot and no user tuning. #130 stages snapshot transport and enforceable ownership; #131 adopts it. Temporary public bridges retire later.

fronts.statement: Status gets 100 ms, ordinary lifecycle 250 ms, admission 5 s. Accepted completion, healthy warm-up, startup silence, worker-output acknowledgement and unacknowledged result retention have no corresponding deadline/eviction here. Silence, retention and idle-accounting changes are deferred.
fronts.reason: The policy record names these distinct purposes and intentional absences; follow-up specs retain the deferred work.

fronts.statement: Resource limits derive from effective constrained/total memory with clamps and hysteresis. Output has chunk/inline/per-result/aggregate bounds; diagnostics and replacements have independent retention/capacity limits. The deeper numeric table is the same seven-family policy.
fronts.reason: The policy record supplies a reason per threshold/recipe; these reasons explain purpose and preservation, not empirical proof that each exact number is optimal.

fronts.statement: Worker wrapper deserializes the complete policy before new Worker. A malformed injected snapshot can now throw in the parent constructor before a worker or its startup handlers exist.
fronts.reason: This source-order consequence accompanies #131 chunk-limit adoption. No separate reason for moving this malformed-input failure boundary was found.

fronts.statement: Admission order is authentication, readiness, resource pause, queue, then duplicate compatibility. Compatibility reads do not mutate the ledger. Authentication disconnects; not-ready/draining/resource-pressure are retry-safe, incompatible is not. Contradictory code/boolean frames are corrupt. The staging request field stays unknown to avoid a CLI type dependency.
fronts.reason: PR #134 centralizes first-failure order and code-derived retry safety while preserving dependency direction.

fronts.statement: Outer failure precedence is resource interruption → result capacity → worker exit (or stopping) → shutdown code → stopping/internal. Worker failures use a separate four-word vocabulary; concrete instanceof facts stay with mechanism owners.
fronts.reason: PR #133 separates domains and makes classification pure while preserving subtype behavior.

fronts.statement: Test adapters can change the stimulus: inline zero may become a positive floor (transport: at least one 64-KiB chunk); a legacy memoryCapBytes option is accepted but not forwarded. Empty-directory assertions may therefore observe an empty directory without a spill.
fronts.reason: Test-only tuning is stated in #131. The exact compatibility floors and ignored option are not separately justified in the supplied record.

fronts.statement: Spool fixtures now coordinate chunk/inline/result limits and enlarge payloads; a capture threshold changes 1→32. The benchmark resource-policy object gains replacement window/limit fields while schemaVersion remains 1. These are test/reporting decisions, alongside production policy.
fronts.reason: No separate rationale for every changed fixture threshold or unversioned benchmark field was located.

fronts.statement: Accepted execute reattachment and result-fetch resume use independent numeric counters. Factory defaults are one reattachment and one fetch per execute attempt; a reattached attempt gets a fresh inner allowance. Neither counter authorizes local replay of accepted work.
fronts.reason: PR #131 explains the two scopes; #142 gives their final execution-client owner. Episode 06 works through the retained identity and fresh capture.

fronts.statement: Control decoders accept JSON; transfer decoders additionally accept flagged binary chunks. Ordinary lifecycle JSON keeps its larger cap; execution control uses the smaller cap. Chunk headers/digests belong to the wire codec; semantic/correlation checks belong to validation.
fronts.reason: PR #137 distinguishes connection purpose, frame capacity and integrity ownership.

fronts.statement: Socket reads are pull-driven and pause after each chunk. Outbound writes keep call-order FIFO under backpressure. Inbound connections each own response/write chains; one connection does not serialize every client.
fronts.reason: PRs #139 and #141 explain demand, ordered writing and connection isolation.

fronts.statement: Lifecycle/status/ack exchanges share correlation, bounded response and cleanup; acknowledgement stays off the general lifecycle requester port. Validation occurs before accepted delivery state. Composition purpose chooses timeouts even for the same ping.
fronts.reason: PR #140 keeps capability and delivery-state distinctions visible.

fronts.statement: Server endpoint probes reuse the socket client. One shutdown promise is shared while force can escalate an ongoing graceful drain. Raw EOF/errors stay separate from authenticated protocol outcomes.
fronts.reason: PRs #139–141 preserve the protocol/mechanism split and concurrent shutdown settlement.

fronts.statement: #143 makes LocalDaemonTransport a required-policy delegate and removes canFrame; injected-component identity tests and a source-mechanism ban protect that boundary. #149 deletes the facade and composes the split owners directly in DaemonTransportFactory. Shared transport-error classification survives the split.
fronts.reason: PRs #140, #143 and #149 explain common error meaning, direct injection, architectural checks and final composition.

fronts.statement: One receiver retains manifest identity, digest progress and the next RECORD offset across fetch connections; each connection gets a fresh decoder. Offset advances after awaited append, never on receipt alone.
fronts.reason: PR #138 gives durable capture and wire framing different lifetimes.

fronts.statement: A reattached execute attempt allocates fresh output and a fresh per-attempt fetch allowance. Both counters are numeric and independent (factory defaults: one fetch and one reattachment). Only eligible authenticated accepted closure can trigger reattachment.
fronts.reason: PRs #131 and #142 explicitly separate the two recovery scopes.

fronts.statement: At the tip, repeated eligible fetch closures can consume the configured allowance; exhausted fetch-ended becomes accepted corruption. Accepted-close reattachment exhaustion preserves the original accepted-close error. This supersedes the intermediate #131 later-completion-error behavior.
fronts.reason: PR #142 says exhaustion retains accepted-corruption behavior; its implementation stores originalAcceptedClose. This page describes the final delta, not #131 as the final transport.

fronts.statement: Manifest/end coordinates, record count, byte count and digest must agree. Failed capture is disposed; successful finish transfers disposal to the caller for replay/ack cleanup. ACK uses a narrow completion-only lifecycle-client capability. Warm capture/storage and controlled failure outputs belong to daemon.
fronts.reason: PRs #138, #142 and #148 specify capture ownership, transfer cleanup and the narrow ACK capability.

fronts.statement: Before accepted completion, only retry-safe transport failure can fall back locally. Once receipt is accepted, completion failure returns controlled warm failure output, not a second local execution.
fronts.reason: The architecture and #148 keep route, output and replay-safety decisions inside the client.

fronts.statement: Ledger entries keep original acceptedAt and queuePosition through queued/running/terminal/acknowledged states. Compatibility includes commandName and canonical request fields; a duplicate never replays acceptance side effects. The ledger remains daemon-lifetime state, with eviction deferred.
fronts.reason: PR #147 explains one immutable identity and daemon-lifetime idempotence; the follow-up spec defers ledger eviction.

fronts.statement: FIFO turn work includes spool finish, ledger completion and ONE read of the currently tracked delivery promise; a resource sample scheduled in finally gates the next turn after success or failure. Normal turn completion does not await every future fetch or ordinary ACK.
fronts.reason: PRs #146–147 specify the latest-stream barrier and turn-boundary sampling. The single lookup is visible in source.

fronts.statement: One generation manager handles startup, execution correlation, replacement, fencing, release and shutdown. Initial protocol readiness is activated after warm sampling; replacement callers share one operation. Graceful close and forced terminate have separate cached promises.
fronts.reason: PR #145 separates generation lifecycle from resource recovery/circuit policy and supports forced interruption of graceful close.

fronts.statement: A replacement starts the next worker before awaiting old-worker termination; readiness is withheld and old-generation exit reports are fenced. Resource interruption classification remains separate from worker-exit classification.
fronts.reason: #145 commits characterize replacement order; its manager and recovery port preserve the explicit handoff.

fronts.statement: Activity is a pure projection of explicit process/clock, queue, worker and last sampled resource values. Replacement generation comes from worker; spoolBytes comes from the last resource sample. Legacy pong can retain fileCount while activity hides it before readiness.
fronts.reason: PR #144 gives specific reasons for each of these data sources and legacy differences.

fronts.statement: Wall and monotonic time stay distinct. The standalone queue default changes from Date.now to daemon monotonic time; the old shipped process already injected monotonic time. Idle reset remains acceptance-based, not readiness- or completion-based.
fronts.reason: Clock ownership and deferring idle changes are stated in #148. No separate reason for the standalone default’s changed clock domain was found.

fronts.statement: Existing SHA-256 canonical request hashing now includes a commandName/request envelope; object sorting, undefined omission and array order are retained. One registry matcher checks identity+instance plus supplied token/owner/revision/time, strengthening some old instance-only comparisons.
fronts.reason: Command identity is explained in #132; registry centralization is named in #148 commits. No separate reason for each strengthened registry expectation was found. The hashing algorithm itself is not new in this stack.

fronts.statement: Attachments get the original acceptance and subscribe to terminal state. The newest tracked attached-delivery promise replaces the previous map entry; settling an older promise cannot remove a newer one. Execution captures the current promise once.
fronts.reason: PR #146 prefers one latest per-request promise over accumulating every duplicate attachment.

fronts.statement: Normal FIFO progress waits for that captured attached stream, not an ordinary ACK. Workspace-deletion handling and shutdown have explicit bounded ACK waits; later fetches do not retroactively extend an already-captured turn barrier.
fronts.reason: The narrow execution/delivery/shutdown coordination is explicit in #146–147 and the final process/session code.

fronts.statement: ACK authenticates the transfer, attempts physical cleanup, records cleanup failure, then logically acknowledges and replies successfully. A missing/corrupt stored completion can instead invalidate its ledger completion and emit internal failure.
fronts.reason: PR #146 explicitly keeps cleanup failure diagnostic rather than withholding protocol success; its delivery owner retains spool-read failure handling.

fronts.statement: Disconnected traces have time/count retention and fenced handles: late events stop once evicted. Trace expiry is not result eviction. Completion storage and accepted identity can outlive a socket and the trace that described it.
fronts.reason: PR #146 separates trace retention from authoritative ledger/spool ownership; the policy plan defers result eviction.

fronts.statement: The final daemon package is an internal-dependency leaf. CLI classifies/composes; TypeScript depends on core; renderer on core+daemon; telemetry stays a leaf. LocalDaemonTransport is gone and its split owners compose package-locally. No new process hop is created.
fronts.reason: The architecture plan locks import direction and retains process/thread topology. #149 replaces the compatibility facade with focused package composition.

fronts.statement: Public paths are exactly root, /process-entry, /worker-entry, /testing. Root declarations are Node-free; DaemonClient starts one dynamic runtime import at construction and retains its promise, including rejection. Optional host policy defaults to currentSystem.
fronts.reason: Node-free facade is stated in #148. No separate reason was found for constructor-start loading, sticky failure or the optional host-policy fallback.

fronts.statement: Lazy routing reads/observes once and stops at the first route: disabled goes local without registry observation; absent starts independently; starting/recovering stay cold; dead/incompatible fall back and trigger; responsive ready goes warm.
fronts.reason: PR #148 explains ordered lazy guards and package-owned routing, so the first choice prevents later observation side effects.

fronts.statement: Authentication remains operation-specific: identify/terminate/kill require instance+token before the ordinary protocol check; ping/stop use protocol+instance; execute/status/fetch/ack also require token. Relocation preserves this partition.
fronts.reason: No separate reason for the retained operation-specific partition was found; it is not a newly introduced bypass.

fronts.statement: The temporary policy-testing export retires after mechanism tests move package-local; serialization methods retire once entries move. Compiler-backed imports/exports/clock/storage inventories replace compatibility aliases and constrain syntax that could cross the boundary.
fronts.reason: The #148 policy plan supplies explicit retirement conditions; #149 supplies the enforcement rationale.

fronts.statement: The inspector exposes parsed diagnostics, instance summaries and spool counts/bytes, with deterministic order. Missing directories yield empty/false/zero; other I/O errors propagate. It skips malformed diagnostic lines, rejects invalid cursors and reads older backups before the active file.
fronts.reason: Read-only observability is stated in #149. No separate reason was located for each filtering/error/order choice.

fronts.statement: CLI diagnostic assertions switch from raw log bytes/rotation to parsed events; skipped malformed lines make parsed absence weaker than raw-byte absence. Seven status and three stop scenarios disappear from those CLI suites; package tests cover some related behavior, not identical witnesses.
fronts.reason: Package observability and moving tests are stated. No per-assertion rationale establishes equivalence for these removed CLI observations.

fronts.statement: The mocked daemon-entry handoff test (including 257-MiB worker limit) is removed. A worker readiness case loses three startup/four result-duration expectations and its CLI-version mismatch case; generic executor and built-entry tests replace the app-specific seam.
fronts.reason: Package-independent actors/executor injection is stated; loss of those exact assertions is not separately justified.

fronts.statement: A serial package Vitest suite, tsx fixture dependency, platform cleanup, and removal of temporary export/lint assertions accompany migration. The temporary export has a retirement reason; that does not supply reasons for every scheduling or assertion change.
fronts.reason: Inspected package/test configuration, #148–149 commits and plans. None gives separate rationale for every listed choice.

fronts.statement: #148 freezes 38 app-local production copies with a source-content digest, normalized across checkout line endings; #149 replaces the temporary freeze with deletion/reachability enforcement. A changed digest must be updated as a unit.
fronts.reason: Staging and line-ending portability are stated in #148 and its commits. No separate reason for the exact aggregate digest strategy was found. This is a source-copy guard, distinct from accepted-request hashing.

fronts.statement: Warm result capture, disposal and controlled failure outputs are package-owned, rather than supplied by the host. Idle timing still resets at acceptance; changing it to readiness/completion is deferred. These lifetimes travel with the mechanism move.
fronts.reason: PR #148 explicitly assigns capture/replay cleanup to the client and preserves acceptance-based idle accounting during extraction. Episodes 06–08 show the consequences.

fronts.statement: Outgoing execute.protocolVersion now comes from the package constant rather than the stored daemon record. Compatible records can yield identical bytes; the changed decision is which authority supplies that field.
fronts.reason: The field-source change is visible in main’s dispatcher and the final client runtime. No separate rationale was located in the inspected record.

pr131_children.statement: Chose required policy slices over optional per-consumer numbers, because omitted composition must not recreate local defaults.
Chose composition-purpose timeout selection over request-kind selection, because status observation and ordinary execution-status requests have distinct deadlines.
Chose independent numeric resume and reattachment counters over one shared boolean, because each reattached execute attempt has its own fetch-resume allowance.
Chose test-only adapters over production compatibility overloads, because tests need small thresholds without restoring runtime tuning seams.
